newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Asian buying of W.African crude re-emerges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Asian buying of W.African crude re-emerges.

text.p: This week's fall in Brent prices has reopened the arbitrage window for West African crudes to move into Asia, with more than 200,000 barrels per day (bpd) of July loading cargoes traded on the spot market in the last few days, traders said.
This is the latest surge in West African crude demand from Asia since early May when China bought 4.5 million barrels of early June loading crudes from Nigeria, Angola and Gabon.

The main buyers this time have been South Korean refiners, who bought three very large crude carriers (VLCC) of West African grades totalling 5.4 million barrels of Qua Iboe and Brass River crude from Nigeria, Djeno crude from Congo, Zafiru from Equitorial Guinea and Cabinda/Nemba from Angola.
Taiwan's state owned Chinese Petroleum Company also bought two million barrels of Nigerian Forcados and Nkossa on the spot market, in addition to its monthly term cargoes.
Traders said China has also been buying this week, but details were difficult to pin down.
Traders saw this week's movement of West African crudes as the tip of the iceberg. More cargoes were expected to be sold into Japan and Thailand as well.
"There is buying interest from Thailand and Japan, and Korea will probably take more," said a trader with a European oil major.
"The demand is more for middle distillate rich crudes such as Forcados," he said.
The price differential between Brent and Dubai has been relatively narrow for the last month, hovering just below 1.00 for August.
The arbitrage was theoretically workable but Asian refiners' interest in West African crude was limited by competitively priced regional crudes.

Now, with the steepening contango in the Brent market -- which sharply narrowed the August Brent/Dubai differential to around 55/65 cents per barrel -- Asia's interest in crudes priced against Brent has been revived.
The narrow Brent/Dubai has raised interest for Yemen crudes also, which use the dated Brent market too.

Yemen's quarterly term prices have risen through the year and just last week it secured buyers for its full availability of 115,000 bpd of Masila and 40,000 bpd of Marib Light covering the third quarter.
Asian demand for West African crudes has risen substantially since last year.
London-based tanker broker Simpson, Spence and Young said overall first quarter sales to Asia were 855,000 bpd.
But West Africa remains a swing supplier to Asian refiners, with only 95,000 b/d actually committed on term, to Taiwan and South Korea refiner Hanwha, traders said.
Most refiners still buy their West African crudes from the spot market.
However, that should change in coming years because of Asia's growing ability to meet demand from regional supplies, analysts said.
In addition, many refining centres, particularly South Korea, have limited desulphurisation capacity, making the low-sulphur West African grades attractive to many buyers.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3301)
